title: Brown Rice with Carrots, Dark Green Vegetables and Tomato Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of brown rice, sautéed carrots, dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach) and a tomato‑based sauce enriched with added fat (vegetable or butter). The combination of whole grains, vegetables and fat provides a balanced mix of carbohydrates, fiber, vitamins and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, giving it more fiber and micronutrients than white rice.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant whose availability increases with cooking.
Dark green vegetables like broccoli, spinach and kale are among the richest sources of vitamin K and folate.
Adding a modest amount of fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from the vegetables.
The dish can be easily adapted to various cuisines by changing spices and the type of sauce.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice and vegetables supply dietary fiber that supports regular digestion and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Rice provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots and dark green vegetables are rich in vitamins A, C, K, as well as potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from carrots help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The added fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and adds satiety.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The added fat increases the dish’s calorie content, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Fat allergies
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain vegetable oils or dairy fats should choose an appropriate fat source.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Some dark green vegetables (e.g., spinach) contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main meal or side. It pairs well with a lean protein (chicken, fish, tofu) and can be topped with seeds (sesame, pumpkin) for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore moisture.
